title: Exercises on とする・とすると・とすれば・としたら
shortTitle: とする・とすると・とすれば・としたら
description: 10 questions on the meaning and structure of とする, the differences among とすると, とすれば, and としたら, and the use of the ～た form, the volitional form, and particles.

questions.question: In the hypothetical use discussed in the article, what does とする primarily do?
options: It adopts the preceding proposition as a premise within the reasoning, without necessarily asserting it as true in the real world.
It indicates how likely the speaker considers the preceding proposition to be.
It necessarily turns a false proposition into a possible one.
It signals that the speaker has decided to accept the preceding proposition as fact.
questions.explanation: The central function of とする is not to indicate how true or probable a proposition is, but to change its role in the discourse. The content is adopted as a premise or operational basis for the reasoning. It may be plausible, false, imaginary, or even already known.

questions.question: The same sentence can mean either “the participation fee is set at 1,000 yen” or “let us assume a participation fee of 1,000 yen” for the purposes of a calculation. What chiefly determines which interpretation applies?
options: Whether the subject of する is expressed or left implicit.
Whether 千円 is intended as an exact or approximate amount.
The context and the purpose of the discourse: the structure may actually establish a value or merely adopt it provisionally within a line of reasoning.
The register: in writing とする establishes an actual decision, whereas in speech it is hypothetical.
questions.explanation: The grammatical form alone does not determine whether a value is actually being fixed or merely assumed. In an organizational context, 参加費を千円とする may establish the actual fee; in an illustrative calculation, the same amount may simply be adopted as a premise. The specific interpretation therefore depends on context.

questions.prompt: P とすると・P とすれば・P としたら
questions.question: Which analysis correctly describes how these three forms are built?
options: とすると, とすれば, and としたら are three independent particles attached directly to P.
In all three forms, P itself is transformed into と, ば, or たら respectively.
Only とすると derives from とする; the other two are independent constructions.
P is first adopted through とする, and する then takes the conditional form と, ば, or たら respectively.
questions.explanation: The structures are [P とする] + と → P とすると, [P とする] + ば → P とすれば, and [P とする] + たら → P としたら. In とすると, the two instances of と therefore have different functions: the first delimits the assumed content, while the second is the conditional と applied to する.

questions.prompt: とすると・とすれば・としたら
questions.question: Which description best captures their typical pragmatic tendencies?
options: とすると is used for real situations, とすれば for probable situations, and としたら for unreal ones.

とすると readily foregrounds what follows from the premise; とすれば foregrounds the acceptance and evaluation of the premise; としたら is particularly well suited to imagined scenarios, questions, and personal reactions.
とすれば is always more formal and is therefore grammatically preferable to the other two.
The three forms have exactly the same function and differ only in style.
questions.explanation: These are pragmatic tendencies, not absolute rules or a fixed scale of probability. とすると readily presents what follows as a consequence of the premise; とすれば makes the acceptance of that premise more prominent; としたら more readily frames a scenario that the speaker or listener is invited to imagine.

questions.prompt: 明日の試験に合格したとする。
questions.question: How should 合格した be understood in this sentence?
options: It proves that the exam has already taken place despite the presence of 明日.
It is grammatically incompatible with reference to a future event.
It indicates that the speaker considers passing the exam highly probable.
The exam is still in the future, but within the hypothetical scenario it is represented as already having been passed.
questions.explanation: The ～た form remains inside the hypothesis. It can place the speaker mentally at a point after the completion of an event that is still future in the real world. For this reason, ～たとする does not necessarily mean hypothesizing about something in the past.

questions.prompt: 行くとしよう ／ 行こうとする
questions.question: Why should these two structures not be confused?
options: としよう is a past form, whereas 行こうとする is a non-past form.
Only 行こうとする contains the verb する.
としよう necessarily expresses a real decision and can never introduce an assumption.

In 行くとしよう, the volitional applies to する and, in the use discussed here, means “let us suppose that we go”; in 行こうとする, the volitional belongs to 行く, and the construction can express an attempt or the imminence of an action.
questions.explanation: The position of the inflection is crucial. 行く + と + しよう contains the volitional form of する, whereas 行こう + とする contains the volitional form of 行く and belongs to a different construction.

questions.prompt: 温度は一定だとする。／ 温度が一定だとする。／ 温度を一定とする。
questions.question: Which analysis correctly distinguishes the roles of は, が, and を in these examples?
options: は, が, and を perform the same function here and can be freely interchanged.
は always marks contrast, が identifies the person making the assumption, and を marks the subject of the hypothesis.
は presents 温度 as the topic; が marks it as the subject within the hypothesized situation; を presents it as the element to which a value or property is assigned.
が and を are equivalent here, while only は changes the structure of the sentence.
questions.explanation: The three formulations may lead to a similar assumption, but they organize the information differently. は topicalizes 温度; が marks it as the subject of the predicate inside the assumed content; を presents it as the element treated as having the value or property expressed after it.

questions.prompt: 雨が降ったら、試合を中止します。／ 雨が降るとしたら、夕方以降だろう。
questions.question: What is the fundamental structural difference between these two sentences?
options: In the second sentence, としたら indicates that rain is considered less likely.
The first refers to the future, whereas the second necessarily refers to the past.
In the first, たら directly links the event to its consequence; in the second, the possibility of rain is first adopted as a premise and the reasoning then proceeds within that scenario.
In the second sentence, としたら is simply a more formal version of たら.
questions.explanation: With ordinary たら, the condition is directly linked to what will happen if it is met. With とする plus a conditional form, an additional level is introduced: the possibility of rain is first framed as a premise and then used as the basis for further reasoning.

questions.prompt: 彼はすでに辞退したらしい。とすれば、次の候補は田中さんだ。
questions.question: What role does とすれば play in this example?
options: It introduces an entirely new hypothesis unrelated to the preceding sentence.
It signals that the speaker considers the information just received to be false.
It turns 次の候補は田中さんだ into the premise of the reasoning.
It picks up the preceding information as a premise and introduces an inference drawn from it.
questions.explanation: とすると, とすれば, and としたら can function anaphorically in discourse: the premise may already have been stated in the preceding sentence. Here とすれば is roughly equivalent to “if so” or “on that basis”.

questions.prompt: とする・とすると・とすれば・としたら
questions.question: Which statement about register is the most accurate?
options: Register preferences exist, but they interact with discourse function: としたら has a strong affinity with conversation and imagined scenarios, とすれば with measured analytical reasoning, and とすると with drawing out the consequences of a premise, without any of them being rigidly restricted to either writing or speech.
としたら belongs exclusively to informal speech and cannot be used in a polite question.
とすれば is always written and formal, whereas とすると is exclusively conversational.
The choice among the four forms depends only on the degree of politeness required.
questions.explanation: Register and communicative function do not coincide. としたら can appear in polite professional questions; とすれば is not confined to writing; とすると is perfectly natural in conversation when speakers reason from a piece of information. These are tendencies of use, not absolute restrictions.
